<!-- assumption-1: body_md -->
\label{ass:time-reg}
For each arm $a$, $(T^a,R^a,C^a)$ is supported on $[0,\tau_0]^3$ and is jointly absolutely continuous on $[0,\tau_0)^3$.
The death time $T^a$ is continuous, so $P(T^a=\tau_0)=0$, while point masses at $\tau_0$ are allowed for $R^a$ and $C^a$.
<!-- end assumption-1 -->
<!-- assumption-2: body_md -->
\label{ass:A-ignore}
Consistency holds, $(T,R,C)=(T^A,R^A,C^A)$ almost surely. 
Moreover, $A\mathrel{\text{{\rotatebox[origin=c]{90}{\resizebox{2.00ex}{1.55ex}{$\vDash$}}}}}(T^0,T^1,R^0,R^1,C^0,C^1)\mid X$, with $e\le P(A=1\mid X)\le1-e$ a.s. for some $e>0$.
<!-- end assumption-2 -->
<!-- assumption-3: body_md -->
\label{ass:C-ignore}
For each arm $a$, $C^a\mathrel{\text{{\rotatebox[origin=c]{90}{\resizebox{2.00ex}{1.55ex}{$\vDash$}}}}} (T^a,R^a)\mid X$.
<!-- end assumption-3 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:no-gain}
Suppose $(T,R)$ is fully observed, $P_{R\mid T}$ is unrestricted,
and $\psi(P)=\psi(P_T)$ is a scalar pathwise differentiable parameter with marginal IF $\varphi_T$.
Then
$ \varphi_{\mathrm{joint}}(T,R)=\varphi_T(T). $
<!-- end theorem-1 -->

<!-- assumption-6: body_md -->
\label{ass:aj-main-integrated}
Assumption~\ref{ass:eif-gain-primitives} holds.
For $\ell=jk\in\mathcal J$, $M_{\ell,i}(t)=N_{\ell,i}(t)-\int_0^tY_{j,i}(u)\,dA_{\ell}(u)$ is square integrable.
Write $q_j(u)=E\{Y_j(u)\}=P_j(u-)G(u-)$, $j=0,1$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(AJ\arabic*)},leftmargin=2em]
\item\label{ajmain:support}
  With $\mathcal T_j=\{u\in(0,\tau]:q_j(u)>0\}$, the infimum of $q_j$ on every compact subset of $\mathcal T_j$ is positive,
  and $\int_0^\tau I\{q_{j(\ell)}(u)=0\}\,dA_\ell(u)=0$.
\item\label{ajmain:inverse}
  For each $\ell$,
\[
   V_\ell^\textsf{AJ}(\tau)= \int_{(0,\tau]}\frac{I\{q_{j(\ell)}(u)>0\}}{q_{j(\ell)}(u)}\,dA_\ell(u)<\infty.
\]
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end assumption-6 -->

<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The Markovian trajectories part of \Cref{ass:Markov-state} is a semiparametric restriction but is not the source of the gain described here.
The IFs of \Cref{thm:eif-main} and the gain identity \eqref{eq:gain} below do not require Markovian transitions.
With non-Markovian data, the AJ remains consistent  and more efficient than the KM, but is not semiparametrically efficient 
\citep{datta2001validity, munch2023targeted}.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- assumption-7: body_md -->
\label{ass:cox-main-primitives}
The training data are i.i.d., Assumption~\ref{ass:eif-gain-primitives}   holds conditionally on $X$.
The model \eqref{eq:cox-main-transition-model} is correctly specified.
In addition: for each $\ell\in\mathcal J$,
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(CX\arabic*)},leftmargin=2em]
  \item\label{cxmain:bounded}  For $K < \infty$,  $\|X\|\le K$ almost surely, and $\|\beta_{\ell,0}\|<R_\ell<\infty$.
  \item The baseline cumulative hazard is supported on the predictable source support and has finite inverse-risk mass:

  \begingroup
  \setstretch{1}
  \setlength{\jot}{0pt}
  \begin{equation} \label{eq:cox-main-source-support}
    \int I\{s_{\ell,0}(u)=0\}d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(u)=0,
    \qquad
    \int\frac{I\{s_{\ell,0}(u)>0\}}{s_{\ell,0}(u)}d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(u)<\infty.
  \end{equation}
  \endgroup
  \item\label{cxmain:information} The Cox information matrix is nonsingular, i.e., for $\bar X_\ell(\beta,u) = {s_\ell^{(1)}(\beta,u)} / {s_\ell^{(0)}(\beta,u)}.$

  \begingroup
  \setstretch{1}
  \setlength{\jot}{0pt}
  \begin{align*} 
    \lambda_{\min}\left\{\int V_\ell(\beta_{\ell,0},u)s_{\ell,0}(u)d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(u)\right\}>0 ,
    \quad
    V_\ell(\beta,u) = \frac{s_\ell^{(2)}(\beta,u)}{s_\ell^{(0)}(\beta,u)} - \bar X_\ell(\beta,u)\bar X_\ell(\beta,u)^\top .
  \end{align*} 
  \endgroup
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end assumption-7 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:cox-main-regime}
Under Assumption~\ref{ass:cox-main-primitives},
$ \text{for each } \ell\in\mathcal J $,
$ \|\widehat\beta_\ell-\beta_{\ell,0}\|=O_p(n^{-1/2}), $\;
$ \sup_{t\le\tau} \big|\widehat\Lambda_{0,\ell}(t)-\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(t)\big| =O_p(n^{-1/2}), $\;
and\; $ \widehat\mu_{n,m}^{\textsf{Cox},\textsf{pi}}(\tau)-\mu_\tau =O_p(m^{-1/2}+n^{-1/2}). $
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- assumption-8: body_md -->
\label{ass:main-transition-martingale-linearization}
For a deterministic sequence $a_N\downarrow0$, suppose that for every fold $k$, relative to the training-sample calendar-time filtration $\mathbb F_{-k}=\{\mathcal F_{-k}(u):0\le u\le\tau\}$,
\begin{align*}
  D_{k,\ell}(u\mid x)
  =
  U_{k,\ell}(u\mid x)+R_{k,\ell}(u\mid x),
  \qquad \ell\in\mathcal J,
\end{align*}
where $U_{k,\ell}(\cdot\mid x)$ is a square-integrable $\mathbb F_{-k}$-martingale and the stochastic Fubini interchanges below are valid.
The process $e_{G,-k}(u,x)$ is left-continuous and $\mathbb F_{-k}$-predictable.
For every bounded $\mathbb F_{-k}$-predictable multiplier $z$, write
$
\|z\|_{2,\infty}
=
\left[
P_X\left\{\sup_{0\le u\le\tau}|z(u,X)|^2\right\}
\right]^{1/2},
$
and define
\begin{align*}
  \mathcal U_{k,z}(t)
  &=
  \sum_{\ell\in\mathcal J}
  P_X\int_0^t
  L_{\ell,0}(u,X)z(u,X)\,dU_{k,\ell}(u\mid X),
\\
  \mathcal R_{k,z}
  &=
  \sum_{\ell\in\mathcal J}
  P_X\int_0^\tau
  L_{\ell,0}(u,X)z(u,X)\,dR_{k,\ell}(u\mid X).
\end{align*}
There are random variables $C_{k,N}=O_p(1)$, uniformly over the fixed number of folds, such that
$
  \langle\mathcal U_{k,z}\rangle(\tau)
  \le C_{k,N}a_N^2\|z\|_{2,\infty}^2,
$ and $ 
  |\mathcal R_{k,z}|
  \le C_{k,N}a_N\|z\|_{2,\infty}.
$
<!-- end assumption-8 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:plugin-onestep-integrated-summary}
Assume conditionally independent censoring.
Suppose that, for some constants $g_0>0$ and $M<\infty$, the event
\begin{align*} 
  \mathcal E_N=
  \bigcap_{k=1}^K
  \left\{
  \begin{array}{l}
    A_0(\cdot\mid x) \text{ and } \widehat A^{(-k)}(\cdot\mid x) \in\mathscr A_\tau(M)\quad \text{for }P_X\text{-a.e. }x,
    \\[2mm]
    G(\cdot\mid x) \text{ and } \widehat G^{(-k)}(\cdot\mid x) \text{ are survival functions},
    \\[1mm]
    \displaystyle\inf_{0\le u\le\tau,\, x}G(u-\mid x)\ge g_0,
    \qquad
    \inf_{0\le u\le\tau,\, x}\widehat G^{(-k)}(u-\mid x)\ge g_0/2
  \end{array}
\right\}
\end{align*} 
satisfies $P(\mathcal E_N)\to1$, where the infima over $x$ are understood $P_X$-essentially.
Suppose that, for a deterministic sequence $c_N\downarrow0$,

\begingroup
\setstretch{1}
\setlength{\jot}{0pt}
\begin{align} \label{eq:main-censoring-rate}
  \max_{1\le k\le K}P_X\{\eta_{-k}(X)^2\}=O_p(c_N^2).
\end{align}
\endgroup
Let $\widehat\mu_N^{\textsf{cf},\textsf{pi}}$ and $\widehat\mu_N^{\textsf{cf},\textsf{os}}$ be the
cross-fitted estimators in \eqref{eq:crossfit-plugin-os-main}, with hazard-induced fold-specific one-step weights.
Then the following statements hold.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\alph*)},leftmargin=2em]
\item \textit{Global one-step robustness.}
The hazard-induced cross-fitted one-step estimator satisfies

\begingroup
\setstretch{1}
\setlength{\jot}{0pt}
\begin{equation} \label{eq:main-os-rate-with-Ghat}
  \widehat\mu_N^{\textsf{cf},\textsf{os}}(\tau)-\mu_\tau
  =
  O_p(N^{-1/2}+c_N).
\end{equation}
\endgroup
This conclusion uses no convergence of the transition learner.

\item \textit{Plug-in rate.}
Suppose, in addition, that for deterministic sequences $a_N,b_N\downarrow0$,

\begingroup
\setstretch{1}
\setlength{\jot}{0pt}
\begin{align} \label{eq:main-plugin-precise-rates}
  \max_{1\le k\le K}P_X\{\delta_{A,-k}(X)^2\}=O_p(a_N^2),
  \qquad
  \max_{1\le k\le K}P_X\{\omega_{-k}(X)\}=O_p(b_N).
\end{align}
\endgroup
Then 
the cross-fitted plug-in estimator satisfies
\begingroup
\setstretch{1}
\setlength{\jot}{0pt}
\begin{align}
  \label{eq:main-plugin-rate}
  \widehat\mu_N^{\textsf{cf},\textsf{pi}}(\tau)-\mu_\tau
  =
  O_p(N^{-1/2}+a_N+b_N).
\end{align}
\endgroup

\item \textit{Local second-order one-step rate.}
Suppose \eqref{eq:main-plugin-precise-rates} and Assumption~\ref{ass:main-transition-martingale-linearization} hold.

<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
A function $\phi\in L^2_0(P)$ is an influence function (IF) for the parameter $\psi(P)$ at $P$,
relative to a model $\mathcal{M}\equiv\{ P \}$, if:
for every regular one-dimensional submodel
$\{  P^{(\epsilon)} \}_{\epsilon\in(-\eta,\eta)}\subset\mathcal{M}$ with a score function
$s(t,r)\equiv\partial_\epsilon\log f^{(\epsilon)}(t,r)\big|_{\epsilon=0} \in L^2_0(P)$,
the pathwise derivative of $\psi$ at $P$ is given by the inner product of the score with $\phi$:
\begin{align*}
  \partial_\epsilon \psi(P^{(\epsilon)})\big|_{\epsilon=0}
  =
  E \{\phi(T,R) s(T,R)\} , \qquad\forall s\in\mathcal{T}_P(\mathcal{M}).
\end{align*}
An IF $\phi\equiv\phi_{P}(t,r)$ is determined jointly by $\psi$ and $\mathcal{M}$, and is an $L^2_0(P)$ function that varies with $P\in\mathcal{M}$.
Geometrically, $\phi_P$ is the $L^2(P)$ gradient of the functional $\psi$ on $\mathcal{M}$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
The semiparametric efficiency bound for $\psi(P)$ relative to $\mathcal{M}$ is
$\inf_{\phi \in \textsf{IF}(\psi,P;\mathcal{M})} E \phi^2(T,R),$
where $\textsf{IF}(\psi,P;\mathcal{M})$ is the set of all influence functions.
The IF that achieves the bound is called the efficient influence function (EIF).
Geometrically, the EIF is the $L^2(P)$ projection of any IF onto $\mathcal{T}_P(\mathcal{M})$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
We use regular parametric submodels in a dominated model.
Let $\mathcal{T}_R$ be the nuisance tangent space corresponding to perturbations of $P_{R|T}$.
Since the conditional law $P_{R|T}$ is unrestricted,
$$
\mathcal{T}_R = \big\{ s(t,r)\in L^2(P) \ ;\ P[s(T,R)\,|\,T]=0 \text{ a.s. } \big\} .
$$
The parameter $\psi(P)$ is invariant under perturbations in $\mathcal{T}_R$.
Its EIF $\phi_P(t,r)$ therefore satisfies $E[\phi_P(T,R) s(T,R)] = 0$ for all $s \in \mathcal{T}_R$,
and hence $\phi_P\in\mathcal{T}^\perp_R$.
The orthogonal complement of $\mathcal{T}_R$ in $L^2_0(P_{T,R})$ consists of the mean-zero functions of the marginal variable with law $P_T$:
$$
\mathcal{T}^\perp_R = \big\{ g(T)\in L^2(P_T)\ ;\ Eg(T) = 0 \big\} .
$$
Consequently, the EIF in $\mathcal{M}$ for $P_{T,R}$ agrees with the EIF in the reduced model $\mathcal{M}_0$ for $P_T$:
$\phi_{P_T}(T)\equiv \phi_{P_{T,R}}(T,R)$ a.s..
The efficiency bounds for $\psi(P_{T,R})$ in $\mathcal{M}$ and $\mathcal{M}_0$ thus coincide.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
For $t<\tau$, use $v(t)=S(\tau)/S(t)$ and
$\mathrm{d}\{1/S(u)\}=\lambda_T(u)\,\mathrm{d}u/S(u)$ in the compensator decomposition to obtain
\begin{align}
  \label{eq:M-theta-bullet}
    \int_0^t-v(u)\,\mathrm{d}M_T^\bullet(u)
    &=-\frac{S(\tau)}{S(T\wedge t)}N_T^*(t)
    +S(\tau)\left\{\frac1{S(T\wedge t)}-1\right\}\notag
    \\
    &=v(t)Y^*(t+)-\theta
    =E\{Y^*_{\tau+}\mid\mathcal F_t^\bullet\}
      -E\{Y^*_{\tau+}\mid\mathcal F_0^\bullet\}
    =M_\theta^\bullet(t).
  \end{align}
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:martingale-representation}
We ignore censoring $C$ in this lemma, and assume that $\mathcal{F}^\bullet$ is generated only by $N^*_T(t)$.
The tangent space $\mathcal{T}_P\equiv\big\{ g\in L^2(P,\mathcal{F}^\bullet) \ ;\ \mathbb{E}g(T)=0 \big\}$
of density score functions has the following characterization.
Define
\[
\mathcal{T}^M_P=
  \bigg\{
    \int_0^\infty h(t) \;\mathrm{d} M^\bullet_T(t)
    \ ;\
    \mathbb{E}h^2(T)=\int_0^\infty h^2(t) S(t) \lambda(t) \;\mathrm{d}t <\infty
  \bigg\} .
\]
Then $\mathcal{T}^M_P=\{g(T)\ ;\ g\in \mathcal{T}_P\}$.
In particular, the full-data IF of $\theta(P)$ can be expressed as:
\begin{equation} \label{eq:IF-M-star}
  \phi^\bullet(T)
  = I(T>\tau) - \theta
  = \int_0^\infty \big\{ I(s>\tau)-v(s)\big\} \;\mathrm{d} M^\bullet_T(s)
  = \int_0^\tau \;\mathrm{d} M^\bullet_\theta(s) .
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
For $h\in L^2(P_T)$, the martingale isometry and Fubini's theorem give
\[
  E\left\{\int_0^\infty h(t)\,\mathrm{d}M_T^\bullet(t)\right\}^{2}
  =\int_0^\infty h(t)^2S(t)\lambda(t)\,\mathrm{d}t
  =Eh(T)^2<\infty.
\]
The integral is $T$-measurable and has mean zero, proving the first inclusion.
Conversely, for $g\in\mathcal T_P$, the closed martingale
$M_g(t):=E\{g(T)\mid\mathcal F_t^\bullet\}$ is square-integrable, with terminal value $g(T)$.
The point-process representation theorem \cite{jacod1975multivariate} gives
$M_g(t)=\int_0^tH(s)\,\mathrm{d} M_T^\bullet(s)$.
Before the single jump, the event history specifies only that $T\ge t$;
thus $H(t)=h(t)Y^*(t)$ for a deterministic $h$.
Since $M_T^\bullet$ has no increments after $T$, this proves the reverse inclusion.
The isometry also gives $Eh(T)^2=Eg(T)^2<\infty$.

To identify $h$, put $V(t):=E\{g(T)\,|\,T>t\}$.
Strictly prior to $T$, $M_g(t)=V(t)$; at $T$, $M_g$ has a jump and takes the value $M_g(T)=g(T)$.
Absolute continuity of the event-time law makes $V$ continuous on the survival support,
so $\Delta M_g(T)=g(T)-V(T)=h(T)$.
For $g(t)=\phi^*(t)=I(t>\tau)-\theta$, the conditional survival probability
$v(t)$ defined above therefore gives $h(t)=I(t>\tau)-v(t)$.
It equals $-v(t)$ on $[0,\tau]$ and zero after $\tau$, proving \eqref{eq:IF-M-star}.
The hazard-score interpretation of $h$ follows from the likelihood differentiation in \eqref{eq:hazard-score}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Let $F=(T,C)$ denote the full data, with law $P_F$, and let $P_V$ denote the observed-data law.
The full-data factorization is
$P_F(\mathrm{d}t,\mathrm{d}c)=f_{T}(t)\mathrm{d}t\times f_{C}(c)\mathrm{d}c .$
The probability of observing $T$, conditional on $T$, is $P\{\Delta=1\,|\,T\}=P\{C>T\,|\,T\}=G(T).$
Thus $P\{\Delta=0\,|\,T\}=1-G(T)$, and the observed-data law is the continuous--discrete mixture
$$
  P_V(\mathrm{d}t,\delta)
  =
  \Big\{ f_T(t)G(t)\mathrm{d}t \Big\}^\delta \cdot
  \bigg\{ I_\emptyset(t)\int_0^\infty [1-G(s)] f_T(s) \; \mathrm{d}s \bigg\}^{1-\delta} .
$$

Fix a full-data score $s_F(t,c)=s_T(t)+s_C(c)$ for $P_F$,
where $s_T(t)=\partial_\epsilon\big|_{\epsilon=0}\log f^{(\epsilon)}_T(t)$,
and $s_C(c)=\partial_\epsilon\big|_{\epsilon=0}\log f^{(\epsilon)}_C(c)$
correspond to the perturbation $f^{(\epsilon)}_{T}(t)f^{(\epsilon)}_{C}(c)$ of $P_F$.
The induced observed-data score $s_V$ is obtained by differentiating each component of the mixture.
When $\Delta=0$,
\[
s_V(\emptyset,0)=\partial_\epsilon\big|_{\epsilon=0}
  \log \int I(c<t) \;\mathrm{d}P^{(\epsilon)}_{T,C}(t,c)
  =
  \int_0^\infty \int_0^t \big\{s_T(t)+s_C(c)\big\} \frac{I(c<t) f_{T,C}(t,c)}{P\{C<T\}} \;\mathrm{d}c \;\mathrm{d}t ,
\]
and, when $\Delta=1$,
\begin{align*}
s_V(t,1)
  =
  \partial_\epsilon\big|_{\epsilon=0}
  \log f^{(\epsilon)}_T(t) G^{(\epsilon)}(t)
  &=
  s_T(t) + \frac{1}{G(t)} \int_t^\infty s_C(c) f_C(c) \;\mathrm{d} c
  .
\end{align*}
Thus $s_V(t,\delta)= L[s_F]\coloneqq E[s_F(T,C)\,|\,V=(t,\delta)]$ is the conditional expectation of the $P_F$ score,
and the induced tangent space at $P_V$ is
\begin{align}
  \mathcal{T}_V
  &=
  \Big\{ s_V(T^\Delta,\Delta) = E[s_T(T)+s_C(C)| T^\Delta,\Delta ]
  \ ;\
  s_T\in L^2_0(P_T),\ s_C\in L^2_0(P_C) \Big\}, \notag \\
\label{eq:score-SV}
  s_V(t,\delta)
  &=
  \delta\cdot \big[s_T(t) + \tilde s_C(t)\big] + (1-\delta)\cdot E[s_T(T)+s_C(C) \,|\, C<T]
\end{align}
where $\tilde s_C(t) =  E[s_C(C) \,|\, C>t] $.
The missing-not-at-random mechanism $\Delta$ gives $s_V(\emptyset,0)\neq 0$.

The functional
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:observed-law-functional}
  \theta(P_V)
  :=
  \int \frac{\delta I(t>\tau)}{G(t)} \;\mathrm{d}P_V(t,\delta)
  =
  \int \frac{I(t>\tau)}{G(t)} f_T(t)G(t) \;\mathrm{d}t
\end{equation}
identifies $\theta(P_F)$. Along a perturbation $P^{(\epsilon)}_F$ with score $s_F$,
\begin{align*}
\partial_\epsilon\theta(P^{(\epsilon)}_V)
  &=
  \int \frac{\delta I(t>\tau)}{G(t)} \{ s_T(t)+\tilde s_C(t) \} \;\mathrm{d}P_V(t,\delta)
    +
    \int \frac{\delta I(t>\tau)}{G(t)} \{ -\tilde s_C(t) \}  \;\mathrm{d}P_V(t,\delta) .
\end{align*}
The $\tilde s_C$ terms cancel. Under the maintained independence assumption,
$\theta(P_V)$ is therefore invariant under perturbations of $G$.

The EIF of $\theta(P_V)$ is a $P_V$-score of the form
$\phi_V(t,\delta)\equiv\delta\cdot \phi_T(t) + (1-\delta)\cdot \phi_0$
for a $P_T$-score $\phi_T$ and $\phi_0\coloneqq{E}[\phi_T(T) \,|\, C<T]$.
Iterated expectation gives $P_V\phi_V=P_T\phi_T=0$.
On $\mathcal{T}_V$, the $L^2(P_V)$ inner product of pairs of scores of the form \eqref{eq:score-SV} is
\begin{align} \label{eq:observed-law-product}
  \langle u_V, v_V \rangle_{P_V}
  &=
  \int \big\{u_T(t)+\tilde u_C(t)\big\}\big\{v_T(t)+\tilde v_C(t)\big\} f_T(t) G(t) \;\mathrm{d} t
  \\
  &\hspace{1cm} + P\{C<T\} \cdot {E}[u_F(T,C)\,|\,C<T]\cdot {E}[v_F(T,C)\,|\,C<T] . \notag
\end{align}
The score components $L[s_T]$ and $L[s_C]$ are not orthogonal.
In particular, the only $s\in\mathcal{T}_V$ orthogonal to $E[s_C(C)\,|\,V]$ is the zero score.
Thus the missing-not-at-random model requires knowledge of $G$ external to the observed $V$ data for identification.

We now restrict attention to $\mathcal{T}_T$, the perturbations of $P_T$. We seek
$\phi_V\in\mathcal{T}_V$ of the form
$\phi_V(t,\delta)=\delta \phi_T(t) + (1-\delta)\phi_0$,
$\phi_0 = \mathbb{E}[\phi_T(T)\,|\,C<T]$, $\phi_T\in L^2_0(P_T)$,
such that, for every $s_T\in \mathcal{T}_F$ inducing \eqref{eq:score-SV},
\[
  P_F\{\phi_Fs_T\} = P_V\{\phi_Vs_V\} ,
  \qquad \forall  s_T\in\mathcal{T}_T,
  \qquad \phi_F(t)=I(t>\tau)-\theta .
\]
The form \eqref{eq:score-SV} does not require $\phi_V$ to be the image of
$\phi_F$; in particular, $\phi_T$ need not equal $\phi_F$.
By \cref{eq:observed-law-functional},
\begin{equation} \label{eq:IF-phiF}
  P_F\{\phi_Fs_F\}
  =
   \int \phi_F(t) s_T(t) \;\mathrm{d}P_F
  =
  \int \frac{\phi_F(t)}{G(t)} s_T(t) G(t) \;\mathrm{d}P_T(t)
\end{equation}
whereas the inner product in \cref{eq:observed-law-product} gives
\begin{align}
  P_V\{\phi_Vs_V\}
  &=
  \int \phi_T(t) s_T(t) G(t)  \;\mathrm{d}P_T(t)
  + \phi_0 \cdot \int
  s_T(t)[1-G(t)]
  \;\mathrm{d}P_T(t) \notag \\
\label{eq:IF-phiV}
  &=
  \int
    \Big\{ \phi_T(t)G(t)
    +
    \phi_0(1-G(t))
    \Big\} s_T(t)
  \;\mathrm{d}P_T(t),
  \qquad\qquad \forall  s_T\in\mathcal{T}_T.
\end{align}
Matching the integrands in \cref{eq:IF-phiF} and \cref{eq:IF-phiV} yields
$\phi_F(t) = \Big\{ \phi_T(t)G(t) + \phi_0 (1-G(t)) \Big\}$, equivalently $\phi_T(t) = \frac{\phi_F(t)}{G(t)} - \frac{\phi_0(1-G(t))}{G(t)}$.
Substituting the preceding expression for $\phi_T$ into
$\phi_0=E\{\phi_T(T)\mid C<T\}$ yields
\[
\phi_0\int\frac{1-G(t)}{G(t)}\,\mathrm{d}P_T(t)
=\int\phi_F(t)\frac{1-G(t)}{G(t)}\,\mathrm{d}P_T(t).
\]
Thus $\phi_0=\int\phi_F(t)\omega(t)\,\mathrm{d}P_T(t)$,
where $\omega(t)\coloneqq\frac{(1-G(t))/G(t)}{\int(1-G(t))/G(t)\,\mathrm{d}P_T(t)}$.
The centering constant is thus a tilted expectation of the full-data IF.
Substitution into the expression for $\phi_T$ gives
\begin{align}
  \phi_T(t)
  &=
  \frac{1}{G(t)} \big\{ \phi_F(t) - \phi_0(1-G(t)) \big\}
  =
  \frac{1}{G(t)} \big\{ \phi_F(t) - \phi_0 \big\} + \phi_0
  \notag \\
  \phi_V(t,\delta)
  &=
  \delta \phi_T(t) + (1-\delta)\phi_0
  =
  \frac{\delta}{G(t)} \big\{ \phi_F(t)-\phi_0\big\} + \phi_0
  =
  \frac{\delta}{G(t)}\phi_F(t) + \Big\{ 1-\frac{\delta}{G(t)} \Big\}\phi_0
  \notag \\
  &=
  \phi_F(t) + \Big\{ \frac{\delta}{G(t)}-1 \Big\} \big\{ \phi_F(t)-\phi_0\big\} .
  \label{eq:IF-phiVortho}
\end{align}
Finally, the decomposition in \cref{eq:IF-phiVortho} is orthogonal:
conditioning the product of its two terms on $T$ gives zero because
$E\{\Delta/G(T)-1\mid T\}=0$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Let $F=(T,C)$ and $O=(\tilde T,\Delta)$, and work under \Cref{ass:time-reg,ass:C-ignore}.
For this proof, let $\mathcal F_t^\bullet=\sigma\{N_T^*(s),N_C^*(s):0\le s\le t\}$ be the joint full-data filtration,
and write $\bm N(t)=(N(t),N_C(t))$ and $Y(t)=I(\tilde T\ge t)$.
The full-data and observed-data likelihoods, \cite{jacod1975multivariate}, are
\begin{align*}
  L^\bullet(\bm N^*)
  &=
  \bigg\{\prod_{0<t\le\tau_0}\lambda(t)^{\mathrm{d}N^*_T(t)} \lambda_C(t)^{\mathrm{d}N^*_C(t)}\bigg\}
  \exp\bigg(-\int_0^{\tau_0}\{\lambda(t)Y^*_T+\lambda_C(t)Y^*_C(t)\}\,\mathrm{d}t\bigg)
  \\
  L^\circ(\bm N)
  &=
  \bigg\{\prod_{0<t\le\tau_0}\lambda(t)^{\mathrm{d}N(t)} \lambda_C(t)^{\mathrm{d}N_C(t)}\bigg\}
  \exp\bigg(-\int_0^{\tau_0}\{\lambda(t)+\lambda_C(t)\}Y(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\bigg).
\end{align*}
For a regular perturbation of the death hazard, define
\begin{equation} \label{eq:hazard-score}
  h(t)\coloneqq\partial_\epsilon\big|_{\epsilon=0}\log\lambda^{(\epsilon)}(t).
\end{equation}
Differentiating the log-likelihood gives the death score
$s^\circ(O)=\partial_\epsilon\log L^{\circ(\epsilon)}(\bm N) =\int_0^{\tau_0}h(t)\,\mathrm{d}M^\circ(t)$.
The corresponding full-data score is $s^\bullet(F)=\int_0^{\tau_0}h(t)\,\mathrm{d}M^\bullet(t)$;
the same calculation applies to the censoring hazard.
Thus the full-data and observed-data tangent spaces have the decompositions
$\mathcal T^\bullet=\mathcal T^\bullet_T\otimes\mathcal T^\bullet_C$ and
$\mathcal T^\circ=\mathcal T^\circ_T\otimes\mathcal T^\circ_C$, respectively, with
\[
\mathcal T^\circ
=\bigg\{
  \int_0^{\tau_0}h_T(t)\,\mathrm{d}M^\circ(t)
  +\int_0^{\tau_0}h_C(t)\,\mathrm{d}M_C^\circ(t) \;:\;
  h_T\in L^2(P_T),\ h_C\in L^2(P_C)
\bigg\}.
\]
The score operator $L[s^\bullet]=E\{ s^\bullet(F)\,|\,O\}$ replaces each full-data martingale integral by its observed-data counterpart.
Absence of simultaneous event and censoring jumps makes the two score components orthogonal.
Perturbing the censoring law does not change the target, although the influence function may depend on that law.

Differentiating $\theta=S(\tau)$ along a death-hazard perturbation gives
\begin{equation} \label{eq:IF-h-product}
  \left.\partial_\epsilon\theta(P^{\circ(\epsilon)})\right|_{\epsilon=0}
  =-S(\tau)\int_0^\tau h(t)\lambda(t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
\end{equation}
For two event-hazard scores, the martingale isometry gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:M-isometry}
  E\big\{s^\circ_1(O)s^\circ_2(O)\big\}
  =E\int_0^{\tau_0}h_1(t)h_2(t)Y(t)\lambda(t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
\end{equation}
Since $E\{Y(t)\}=S(t)G(t)$ and $v(t)=S(\tau)/S(t)$ for $t\le\tau$,
matching \eqref{eq:IF-h-product} with \eqref{eq:M-isometry} gives
$b(t)=-v(t)/G(t)$ on $[0,\tau]$ and zero thereafter.
This representer lies in the event-score tangent space and is orthogonal to the censoring scores.
Hence
\begin{equation} \label{eq:IF-Va-M}
  \phi^\circ(O)=\int_0^\tau\frac{-v(t)}{G(t)}\,\mathrm{d}M^\circ(t)
  =\int_0^\tau\frac{Y_C^*(t)}{G(t)}\,\mathrm{d}M_\theta^\bullet(t),
\end{equation}
where the last equality uses stopping at censoring and \eqref{eq:M-theta-bullet}.

For the augmentation representations, put $U(t)=I(C>t)/G(t)$ and $V(t)=M_\theta^\bullet(t)$.
The product rule is
\begin{equation} \label{eq:UV-integration}
  \mathrm{d}[UV](t)=U(t-)\mathrm{d}V(t)+V(t-)\mathrm{d}U(t)
  +\mathrm{d}[U,V](t).
\end{equation}
Here
$\mathrm{d}U(t)=I(C\ge t)\,\mathrm{d}\Lambda_C(t)/G(t) -\mathrm{d}N_C^*(t)/G(t)=-\mathrm{d}M_C^\bullet(t)/G(t)$ and
$\mathrm{d}V(t)=-v(t)\,\mathrm{d}M^\bullet(t)$.
The cross-variation vanishes because the event and censoring processes have no simultaneous jumps.
Therefore
\begin{equation} \label{eq:UV-formula}
  \mathrm{d}\left\{\frac{I(C>t)M_\theta^\bullet(t)}{G(t)}\right\}
  =\frac{I(C\ge t)}{G(t)}\,\mathrm{d}M_\theta^\bullet(t)
  -\frac{M_\theta^\bullet(t-)}{G(t)}\,\mathrm{d}M_C^\bullet(t).
\end{equation}
The initial product is zero. At $\tilde T\wedge\tau$, it is
$I(C>\tilde T\wedge\tau)\phi^*(\tilde T)/G(\tilde T\wedge\tau)$:
the indicator removes the censored cases in which the score martingale has not yet reached its terminal value.
Integrating \eqref{eq:UV-formula} to this endpoint and setting
$\Delta_{C,\tau}=I(C>\tilde T\wedge\tau)$ yields
\begin{equation} \label{eq:IF-circ-two}
  \phi^\circ(O)=\frac{\Delta_{C,\tau}}{G(\tilde T\wedge\tau)}\phi^*(\tilde T)
  +\int_0^{\tilde T\wedge\tau}
  \frac{M_\theta^\bullet(t-)}{G(t)}\,\mathrm{d}M_C^\bullet(t).
\end{equation}
The stopped interval of integration is essential for $\mathcal{F}^\circ$-measurability:
after $T$ the centered score martingale is constant but need not be zero,
so the full-data censoring integral without stopping need not be a function of $O$.

We develop a second augmented IF representation.
Use the product identity \eqref{eq:UV-integration} with
$V(t)=M_\theta^\bullet(t)+\theta=v(t)Y_T^*(t+)$.
The differentials are unchanged, while the boundary products at $0$ and
$\tau$ are $\theta$ and $I(C>\tau)I(T>\tau)/G(\tau)$.
Thus
\begin{equation} \label{eq:UV-MMC}
  \frac{I(C>\tau)I(T>\tau)}{G(\tau)}-\theta
  =\int_0^\tau\frac{-v(t)Y_C^*(t)}{G(t)}\,\mathrm{d}M^\bullet(t)
  -\int_0^\tau\frac{v(t)Y_T^*(t)}{G(t)}\,\mathrm{d}M_C^\bullet(t).
\end{equation}
Substitution of \eqref{eq:IF-Va-M} gives
\[
  \phi^\circ(O)=\frac{I(\tilde T>\tau)}{G(\tau)}-\theta
  +\int_0^\tau\frac{M_\theta^\bullet(t-)+\theta}{G(t)}\,\mathrm{d}M_C^\circ(t).
\]
Here $M_\theta^\bullet(t-)+\theta=v(t)Y_T^*(t)$ vanishes after death,
which permits the observed censoring martingale increments on $[0,\tau]$.

Finally, \eqref{eq:M-isometry} and independence of $T,C$ give
\[
\mathbb V\{\phi^\circ(O)\}
=\int_0^\tau\frac{v(t)^2S(t)G(t)\lambda(t)}{G(t)^2}\,\mathrm{d}t
=\theta^2\int_0^\tau\frac{\lambda(t)}{S(t)G(t)}\,\mathrm{d}t.
\]
The two martingale terms in \eqref{eq:UV-MMC} are orthogonal, and the
isometry gives the censoring term variance
$\theta^2\int_0^\tau\lambda_C(t)/\{S(t)G(t)\}\,\mathrm{d}t$.
Since $P(\tilde T>\tau)=S(\tau)G(\tau)$, the variance of its left side is
$\theta/G(\tau)-\theta^2$.
Subtracting proves the second expression:
\[
  \mathbb V\{\phi^\circ(O)\}
  =\frac{\theta}{G(\tau)}-\theta^2
  -\theta^2\int_0^\tau\frac{\lambda_C(t)}{S(t)G(t)}\,\mathrm{d}t.
\]
<!-- end proof-5 -->

Integrating \cref{eq:UM-theta} from
$t=0$ to $t=T\wedge\tau$ gives $\int_0^{T\wedge\tau} \;\mathrm{d}Z(t)=Z(T\wedge\tau)-Z(0)$ on the left.
At $t=0$, the boundary value is $Z(0)=1/1\cdot M^*_\theta(0)=0$; at $t=T\wedge\tau$,
it is $Z(T\wedge\tau) = \frac{\Delta_{C,\tau}}{G(T\wedge\tau)}[I(T>\tau)-\theta]$,
with $\Delta_{C,\tau}=I(C>T\wedge\tau)$,
where $\phi^*$ is observed only when $\Delta_{C,\tau}$ holds and is weighted by the inverse probability of that event.

<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:product-integral-expansion}
Let $A,B\in\mathscr A_{\tau}$, $D=B-A$, and
$0\le s\le t\le\tau$.  Then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:duhamel}
P_B(s,t)-P_A(s,t)=
\int_{(s,t]}P_A(s,u-)\,d\mathbf D(u)\,P_B(u,t),
\end{equation}
and also the left-hand variation-of-constants form
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:duhamel-left}
P_B(s,t)-P_A(s,t)=
\int_{(s,t]}P_B(s,u-)\,d\mathbf D(u)\,P_A(u,t).
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{align}
\label{eq:product-integral-second-order}
P_B(s,t)-P_A(s,t)
&=
\int_{(s,t]}P_A(s,u-)\,d\mathbf D(u)\,P_A(u,t)
+R_{A,B}^{\mathrm{PI}}(s,t), \\
\label{eq:product-integral-remainder}
R_{A,B}^{\mathrm{PI}}(s,t)
&=
\int_{(s,t]}\int_{(u,t]}
P_A(s,u-)\,d\mathbf D(u)\,P_A(u,v-)\,d\mathbf D(v)\,P_B(v,t).
\end{align}
Moreover, if
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:product-integral-mass-bound}
|A|_{\tau}\vee |B|_{\tau}\le M<\infty,
\end{equation}
then there is a finite constant $C_{\mathrm{PI}}(M,\tau)$ such that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:product-integral-lipschitz}
\kappa_{\mathrm{PI}}(A,B)
\le C_{\mathrm{PI}}(M,\tau)\left\lVert D\right\rVert_{\infty,\tau}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
First suppose that $A$ and $B$ are step functions on a common grid
$s=t_0<\cdots<t_q=t$. Set $F_r=I+\Delta_r\mathbf A$,
$G_r=I+\Delta_r\mathbf B$, and $K_r=G_r-F_r=\Delta_r\mathbf D$;
write $F_{a:b}=F_a\cdots F_b$ and $G_{a:b}=G_a\cdots G_b$, with an empty
product equal to $I$. Telescoping gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:finite-telescope}
G_{1:q}-F_{1:q}=\sum_{a=1}^qF_{1:a-1}K_aG_{a+1:q}.
\end{equation}
Take refining partitions whose mesh tends to zero and which contain all
jumps larger than the inverse partition index. The finite-variation
construction gives uniform convergence of the Euler products, while the
sum in \eqref{eq:finite-telescope} converges to the Stieltjes integral
with factors $P_A(s,u-)$ and $P_B(u,t)$. This proves
\eqref{eq:duhamel}, with the displayed left-limit convention.
Interchanging $A$ and $B$ gives \eqref{eq:duhamel-left}.
Adding and subtracting $P_A(u,t)$ in \eqref{eq:duhamel}, and applying
the same identity on $(u,t]$ to the difference $P_B(u,t)-P_A(u,t)$,
gives \eqref{eq:product-integral-second-order}--\eqref{eq:product-integral-remainder}.

For the modulus bound, first note that the signed matrix measure
\[
d\mathbf D(u)=
\begin{pmatrix}
-(dD_{01}+dD_{02}) & dD_{01} & dD_{02}\\
0&-dD_{12}&dD_{12}\\
0&0&0
\end{pmatrix},
\]
satisfies the row-wise absolute-measure bound
$\left\lVert d\mathbf D(u)\right\rVert_\infty \le 2\,d|D_{01}|(u)+2\,d|D_{02}|(u)+2\,d|D_{12}|(u) =2\,dV_D(u)$,
where $dV_D=d|D_{01}|+d|D_{02}|+d|D_{12}|$. Assume now \eqref{eq:product-integral-mass-bound}. By the preceding
Euler-product approximation, it suffices to obtain a bound uniform over
finite grids. Each scalar entry of $G_{1:q}-F_{1:q}$ in
\eqref{eq:finite-telescope} is a finite sum of terms
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:product-integral-scalar-sum}
    \sum_{a=1}^q c_a x_a,
\end{equation}
Here $x_a$ is one of $\Delta D_{01}(t_a)$, $\Delta D_{02}(t_a)$, or $\Delta D_{12}(t_a)$, and $c_a$ is a
scalar entry of
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:product-integral-coefficient}
    C_a=F_{1:a-1}E_rG_{a+1:q},
\end{equation}
where $E_r$ ranges over the fixed elementary matrices associated with the
three transitions. Set $X_a=\sum_{b=1}^a x_b, \qquad E_x=\max_{0\le a\le q}|X_a|.$ Since $x_a$ is an increment of a
component of $D$ over $[s,t]$, we have $X_a=D_\ell(t_a)-D_\ell(s)$ and hence
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:partial-sum-bound}
    E_x\le 2\left\lVert D\right\rVert_{\infty,\tau}.
\end{equation}
The factor two is absorbed into the final constant. With $c_{q+1}=0$, Abel
summation gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:abel-summation}
\sum_{a=1}^q c_a x_a
=\sum_{a=1}^q c_a(X_a-X_{a-1})
=\sum_{a=1}^q(c_a-c_{a+1})X_a,
\end{equation}
and therefore
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:abel-summation-bound}
\left|\sum_{a=1}^q c_a x_a\right|
\le E_x\left\{|c_q|+\sum_{a=1}^{q-1}|c_a-c_{a+1}|\right\}.
\end{equation}

It remains to bound the coefficient variation. Write $C_a$ for the matrix
in \eqref{eq:product-integral-coefficient}. Row-stochasticity of the $F$- and
$G$-products implies
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:coefficient-terminal-bound}
\left\lVert C_q\right\rVert_\infty=\left\lVert F_{1:q-1}E_r\right\rVert_\infty\le C_0,
\end{equation}
where $C_0$ depends only on the fixed elementary matrices. For $a=1,\ldots,q-1$,
\begin{align}
\label{eq:coefficient-increment}
C_a-C_{a+1}
&=F_{1:a-1}E_rG_{a+1:q}-F_{1:a}E_rG_{a+2:q} \\
&=F_{1:a-1}\{E_rG_{a+1}-F_aE_r\}G_{a+2:q} \notag \\
&=F_{1:a-1}\{E_r(G_{a+1}-I)-(F_a-I)E_r\}G_{a+2:q}. \notag
\end{align}
Row-stochasticity and boundedness of the elementary matrices then give
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:coefficient-increment-bound}
\left\lVert C_a-C_{a+1}\right\rVert_\infty
\le C_0\left\{\left\lVert G_{a+1}-I\right\rVert_\infty+\left\lVert F_a-I\right\rVert_\infty\right\}.
\end{equation}
The one-step factors satisfy
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:product-factor-bound}
\left\lVert F_a-I\right\rVert_\infty\le 2\{\Delta A_{01}(t_a)+\Delta A_{02}(t_a)+\Delta A_{12}(t_a)\},
\end{equation}
with the corresponding bound for $G_{a+1}-I$ obtained with $B$
in place of $A$. Summing \eqref{eq:coefficient-increment-bound} over $a$ and using
$|A|_{\tau}\vee |B|_{\tau}\le M$ yields
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:coefficient-variation-bound}
    \left\lVert C_q\right\rVert_\infty+
    \sum_{a=1}^{q-1}\left\lVert C_a-C_{a+1}\right\rVert_\infty
    \le C(M,\tau).
\end{equation}
This also bounds the variation of each scalar entry $c_a$ of $C_a$.
Combining \eqref{eq:product-integral-scalar-sum}--\eqref{eq:coefficient-variation-bound}
and summing over the finitely many matrix entries and transition coordinates,
we obtain
$\left\lVert P_B(s,t)-P_A(s,t)\right\rVert_\infty \le C_{\mathrm{PI}}(M,\tau)\left\lVert D\right\rVert_{\infty,\tau}$.
Taking the supremum over $0\le s\le t\le\tau$ proves \eqref{eq:product-integral-lipschitz}
on the grid. The constants are independent of the grid, so the preceding
approximation extends the bound to general cadlag finite-variation hazards.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:rmst-hazard-derivative}
Let $A,B\in\mathscr A_{\tau}$ and $D=B-A$.  Write
$M_{\tau}(A):=\mu_A(\tau).$
Throughout the paper,
$\dot\mu_{\tau,A}[D]$ denotes the first-order pathwise derivative of the
deterministic RMST map $M_{\tau}$ at the hazard triplet $A$, evaluated in
the signed finite-variation direction $D$.  Equivalently, if
$A_\varepsilon=A+\varepsilon D$ is an admissible finite-variation path for small
$\varepsilon$, then
$\dot\mu_{\tau,A}[D] =\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}M_{\tau}(A_\varepsilon) \right|_{\varepsilon=0}.$
The paper uses the following explicit Stieltjes representation as the definition of
this derivative for all signed finite-variation directions $D$:
\begin{align}
\label{eq:rmst-pathwise-derivative}
\dot\mu_{\tau,A}[D]
&=
\int_{(0,\tau]}
P^A_0(u-)
\{V^A_1(u,\tau)-V^A_0(u,\tau)\}
\,dD_{01}(u) \\
&\quad-
\int_{(0,\tau]}
P^A_0(u-)V^A_0(u,\tau)\,dD_{02}(u) \notag \\
&\quad-
\int_{(0,\tau]}
P^A_1(u-)V^A_1(u,\tau)\,dD_{12}(u). \notag
\end{align}
Thus $\dot\mu_{\tau,A}[D]$ is a scalar linear functional of the three signed
hazard increments $(dD_{01},dD_{02},dD_{12})$.  It is the linear term in the RMST
expansion
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:rmst-first-order-expansion}
\mu_B(\tau)-\mu_A(\tau)=\dot\mu_{\tau,A}[D]+r_{A,B},
\end{equation}
with remainder satisfying
$|r_{A,B}|\le \tau\omega_{\mathrm{PI}}(A,B)$.
Also,
$|\mu_B(\tau)-\mu_A(\tau)| \le 2\tau\kappa_{\mathrm{PI}}(A,B).$
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
For $t\in[0,\tau]$, Lemma~\ref{lem:product-integral-expansion} gives
\begin{align}
\label{eq:survival-first-order-expansion}
\Psi_t(B)-\Psi_t(A)
&=e_0^\top\int_{(0,t]}P_A(0,u-)\,d\mathbf D(u)P_A(u,t)a_{\mathrm{surv}}+\rho_t,\\
\label{eq:survival-remainder-bound}
|\rho_t|&\le\omega_{\mathrm{PI}}(A,B).
\end{align}
Write $P_j^A(u-)=P_{0j}^A(0,u-)$ and
$v^A(u,t)=P_A(u,t)a_{\mathrm{surv}}=(v_0^A(u,t),v_1^A(u,t),0)^\top$.
Multiplying the transition-hazard matrix by this vector yields
\begin{align}
\label{eq:survival-derivative}
D\Psi_{t,A}[D]
&:=e_0^\top\int_{(0,t]}P_A(0,u-)\,d\mathbf D(u)P_A(u,t)a_{\mathrm{surv}}\notag\\
&=\int_{(0,t]}P_0^A(u-)\{v_1^A(u,t)-v_0^A(u,t)\}\,dD_{01}(u)\notag\\
&\quad-\int_{(0,t]}P_0^A(u-)v_0^A(u,t)\,dD_{02}(u)
      -\int_{(0,t]}P_1^A(u-)v_1^A(u,t)\,dD_{12}(u).
\end{align}
Each scalar coefficient has absolute value at most one by
\eqref{eq:v-bounds}, and
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:rmst-fubini-bound}
\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal J}\int_0^\tau\int_{(0,t]}d|D_\ell|(u)\,dt
=\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal J}\int_{(0,\tau]}(\tau-u)\,d|D_\ell|(u)
\le\tau\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal J}|D_\ell|([0,\tau])<\infty.
\end{equation}
Fubini's theorem for finite signed measures therefore permits integration
of \eqref{eq:survival-derivative} in $t$. The inner integrals are $V_1^A-V_0^A$,
$V_0^A$, and $V_1^A$, respectively, proving
\eqref{eq:rmst-pathwise-derivative}.
Integrating \eqref{eq:survival-first-order-expansion} gives
$r_{A,B}=\int_0^\tau\rho_t\,dt$ and
$|r_{A,B}|\le\tau\omega_{\mathrm{PI}}(A,B)$.
Finally,
$|\Psi_t(B)-\Psi_t(A)|\le2\|P_B(0,t)-P_A(0,t)\|_\infty$,
so integration proves
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:rmst-product-integral-bound}
|\mu_B-\mu_A|\le2\tau\kappa_{\mathrm{PI}}(A,B).
\end{equation}
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:aj-jump-regularity}
Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:time-reg}, \ref{ass:C-ignore}, \ref{ass:Markov-state}, and~\ref{ass:aj-main-integrated}, let $R_i$ be the latent recurrence time and $T_i$
the latent terminal event time.  Define the transition times
\[
S_{01,i}=\begin{cases}R_i, & R_i<T_i,\\ \infty, & R_i\ge T_i,\end{cases}
\qquad
S_{02,i}=\begin{cases}T_i, & T_i<R_i,\\ \infty, & T_i\ge R_i,\end{cases}
\qquad
S_{12,i}=\begin{cases}T_i, & R_i<T_i,\\ \infty, & R_i\ge T_i.\end{cases}
\]
Then the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\roman*)}]
\item The true transition compensators are continuous:
$\Delta A_{\ell,0}(u)=0, \qquad 0<u\le\tau, \qquad \ell\in\mathcal J .$
\item The total transition-hazard masses are finite and
$A_0\in\mathscr A_{\tau}$.
\item The Nelson--Aalen estimator is row-admissible pathwise:
$\widehat A^{\textsf{AJ}}\in\mathscr A_{\tau}$ for every sample for which the displayed
risk-set ratios are defined with the convention $J_j/\bar Y_j=0$ on
$\{\bar Y_j=0\}$.
\item There are no common calendar-time observed transition jumps in the sample:
\[
J_n^{\max}
    :=\max_{0<u\le\tau}
      \sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal J}\Delta N_{\ell,i}(u)
    \le 1
    \qquad\textnormal{almost surely}.
\]
Consequently $J_n^{\max}=O(1)=o(\sqrt n)$ almost surely.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Assumptions~\ref{ass:time-reg}, \ref{ass:C-ignore}, and~\ref{ass:Markov-state}
imply $\Pr(R_i=T_i)=0$. Thus a subject cannot have simultaneous recurrence and
terminal-event jumps. When both events occur, their times are $R_i$ and
$T_i$ with $R_i<T_i$; when death precedes recurrence, the only observed
transition is $0\to2$. Censoring may remove a transition but cannot create one.

The same assumptions exclude ties between subjects: for $i\ne k$ and
$\ell,r\in\mathcal J$,
$\Pr\{S_{\ell,i}=S_{r,k}<\infty\}=0.$
A finite union over subject and transition pairs gives
$\Pr\{\exists i\ne k,\exists\ell,r,\ S_{\ell,i}=S_{r,k}<\infty\}=0.$
Together with the absence of within-subject simultaneous jumps, this yields
$J_n^{\max}\le1$ almost surely.

For continuity of the compensators, fix $\ell=(j,k)$ and $u\in(0,\tau]$. The absence
of atoms in $S_{\ell,i}$ implies
$\Pr\{\Delta N_{\ell,i}(u)=1\}=0 .$
Taking expectations in the Doob--Meyer decomposition gives
$0=E\{\Delta N_{\ell,i}(u)\} =E\{Y_{j,i}(u)\}\Delta A_{\ell,0}(u) =q_j(u)\Delta A_{\ell,0}(u).$
When $q_j(u)>0$, we obtain $\Delta A_{\ell,0}(u)=0$. When $q_j(u)=0$, the source-support
condition in Assumption~\ref{ass:aj-main-integrated}\ref{ajmain:support}
gives
$\Delta A_{\ell,0}(u) \le \int_0^{\tau}\mathbf 1\{q_j(v)=0\}\,dA_{\ell,0}(v)=0 .$
Hence $A_{\ell,0}$ is continuous. Since $0\le q_j\le1$,
\[
A_{\ell,0}(\tau)
=\int_{(0,\tau]}\mathbf 1\{q_j(u)>0\}\,dA_{\ell,0}(u)
\le
\int_{(0,\tau]}
\frac{\mathbf 1\{q_j(u)>0\}}{q_j(u)}\,dA_{\ell,0}(u)<\infty .
\]
The true hazards therefore have finite mass, and continuity ensures their
row constraints, so $A_0\in\mathscr A_{\tau}$.

Finally, fix a time $u$ and source state $j$. The outgoing
Nelson--Aalen increment from row $j$ is the number of transitions from
subjects at risk in state $j$ just before $u$, divided by the
row-$j$ risk-set size, with value zero for an empty risk set. This
ratio lies in $[0,1]$ because each at-risk subject contributes at most one
outgoing transition. Thus the row constraints defining $\mathscr A_{\tau}$ hold
pathwise for $\widehat A^{\textsf{AJ}}$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:aj-rmst-linearization}
Under Assumption~\ref{ass:aj-main-integrated},
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:aj-rmst-linearization}
\widehat\mu^{AJ}-\mu_0
=
\dot\mu_{\tau,A_0}[\widehat A^{\textsf{AJ}}-A_0]+o_p(n^{-1/2}).
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
We use the left-hand product-integral identity to express the RMST remainder
as a stochastic integral with a predictable integrand, and then bound its
Doob--Meyer components. Set
$\widehat{\mathbf A}^{\textsf{AJ}}(t)=\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal J}\mathbf B_\ell \widehat A^{\textsf{AJ}}_\ell(t)$, $\mathbf A_0(t)=\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal J}\mathbf B_\ell A_{\ell,0}(t)$, $\mathbf D_n=\widehat{\mathbf A}^{\textsf{AJ}}-\mathbf A_0$.
For a transition $\ell$, write $j=j(\ell)$ and
$D_{n\ell}(t)=\widehat A^{\textsf{AJ}}_\ell(t)-A_{\ell,0}(t).$
The decomposition $d\bar N_\ell=d\bar M_{\ell,0}+\bar Y_j\,dA_{\ell,0}$ gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:na-error-decomposition}
D_{n\ell}(t)=U_{n\ell}(t)+Z_{n\ell}(t),
\end{equation}
where
$U_{n\ell}(t)=\int_{(0,t]}\frac{J_j(u)}{\bar Y_j(u)}\,d\bar M_{\ell,0}(u)$, $Z_{n\ell}(t)=\int_{(0,t]}\{J_j(u)-1\}\,dA_{\ell,0}(u)$.
and $J_j/\bar Y_j=0$ on $\{\bar Y_j=0\}$.

We first establish the bounds
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:na-sup-rate}
    \max_{\ell\in\mathcal J}\sup_{t\le\tau}|D_{n\ell}(t)|=O_p(n^{-1/2}),
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:zero-risk-variation}
    \max_{\ell\in\mathcal J}|Z_{n\ell}|(\tau)=O_p(n^{-1}).
\end{equation}
Since $Z_{n\ell}$ is nonincreasing,
$|Z_{n\ell}|(\tau)=\int_{(0,\tau]} \1\{\bar Y_j(u)=0\}\,dA_{\ell,0}(u).$
Consequently,
\begin{align}
\label{eq:zero-risk-expectation-bound}
E|Z_{n\ell}|(\tau)
&\le \int_{(0,\tau]}P\{\bar Y_j(u)=0\}\,dA_{\ell,0}(u) \\
&\le \int_{(0,\tau]}e^{-nq_j(u)}\,dA_{\ell,0}(u)
\le \frac{1}{n}\int_{(0,\tau]}
\frac{\1\{q_j(u)>0\}}{q_j(u)}\,dA_{\ell,0}(u)=O(n^{-1}), \notag
\end{align}
where Assumption~\ref{ass:aj-main-integrated} excludes hazard mass on
$\{q_j=0\}$. The predictable quadratic variation of the martingale component
satisfies
$\langle U_{n\ell}\rangle(t) \le \frac{1}{n}\int_{(0,t]}\frac{J_j(u)}{\bar Y_j(u)}\,dA_{\ell,0}(u)$.
For $B\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,q)$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:binomial-inverse-bound}
    E\left\{\frac{\1(B>0)}{B/n}\right\}
    =nE\left\{\frac{\1(B>0)}{B}\right\}
    \le \frac{C}{q},
    \qquad 0<q\le1,
\end{equation}
with a universal constant $C$. Thus
$E\langle U_{n\ell}\rangle(\tau) \le \frac{C}{n}\int_{(0,\tau]} \frac{\1\{q_j(u)>0\}}{q_j(u)}\,dA_{\ell,0}(u)=O(n^{-1}).$
Doob's $L_2$ inequality now yields
$E\sup_{t\le\tau}|U_{n\ell}(t)|^2 \le 4E\langle U_{n\ell}\rangle(\tau)=O(n^{-1}).$
Together with \eqref{eq:zero-risk-expectation-bound}, this establishes
\eqref{eq:na-sup-rate} and implies
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:aj-hazard-mass-bound}
    |\widehat A^{\textsf{AJ}}|_{\tau}=O_p(1).
\end{equation}

Apply \eqref{eq:duhamel-left} with $A=A_0$, $B=\widehat A^{\textsf{AJ}}$, and $H=\widehat A^{\textsf{AJ}}-A_0$.
Multiplication by $e_0^\top$ and $a_{\mathrm{surv}}$, followed by integration in
$t$ and Stieltjes--Fubini, gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:aj-exact-rmst-identity}
\widehat\mu^{\textsf{AJ}}-\mu_0
=\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal J}\int_{(0,\tau]}L_{n\ell}(u)\,dD_{n\ell}(u),
\end{equation}
where
$L_{n\ell}(u) =\int_u^{\tau} e_0^\top P_{\widehat A^{\textsf{AJ}}}(0,u-)\mathbf B_\ell P_{A_0}(u,t)a_{\mathrm{surv}}\,dt .$
Define the deterministic coefficient
$L_{0\ell}(u) =\int_u^{\tau} e_0^\top P_{A_0}(0,u-)\mathbf B_\ell P_{A_0}(u,t)a_{\mathrm{surv}}\,dt .$
Lemma~\ref{lem:rmst-hazard-derivative} gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:aj-rmst-derivative}
\dot\mu_{\tau,A_0}[\widehat A^{\textsf{AJ}}-A_0]
=\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal J}\int_{(0,\tau]}L_{0\ell}(u)\,dD_{n\ell}(u).
\end{equation}
Subtracting \eqref{eq:aj-rmst-derivative} from
\eqref{eq:aj-exact-rmst-identity}, we obtain
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:aj-predictable-remainder}
\widehat\mu^{\textsf{AJ}}-\mu_0-\dot\mu_{\tau,A_0}[\widehat A^{\textsf{AJ}}-A_0]
=\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal J}\int_{(0,\tau]}\Delta L_{n\ell}(u)\,dD_{n\ell}(u),
\end{equation}
where $\Delta L_{n\ell}=L_{n\ell}-L_{0\ell}$.

To bound the coefficient error, let
$\kappa_n=\sup_{0\le u\le\tau} \|P_{\widehat A^{\textsf{AJ}}}(0,u)-P_{A_0}(0,u)\|_\infty .$
By \eqref{eq:row-stoch} and $\|a_{\mathrm{surv}}\|_\infty=1$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:aj-coefficient-error-bound}
    \max_{\ell\in\mathcal J}\sup_{u\le\tau}|\Delta L_{n\ell}(u)|
    \le C\tau \kappa_n .
\end{equation}
On $\{|A_0|_{\tau}\vee |\widehat A^{\textsf{AJ}}|_{\tau}
\le M\}$, Lemma~\ref{lem:product-integral-expansion} implies
$\kappa_n\le C_M\max_{\ell\in\mathcal J}\sup_{u\le\tau}|D_{n\ell}(u)|.$
Combining this with \eqref{eq:na-sup-rate} and
\eqref{eq:aj-hazard-mass-bound} yields
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:aj-product-integral-rate}
    \kappa_n=O_p(n^{-1/2}),
    \qquad
    \max_{\ell}\sup_{u}|\Delta L_{n\ell}(u)|=O_p(n^{-1/2}).
\end{equation}
The decomposition \eqref{eq:na-error-decomposition} separates the remainder in
\eqref{eq:aj-predictable-remainder} into
$R_{U,n}=\sum_{\ell}\int\Delta L_{n\ell}\,dU_{n\ell}$, $R_{X,n}=\sum_{\ell}\int\Delta L_{n\ell}\,dZ_{n\ell}$.
By \eqref{eq:aj-coefficient-error-bound} and \eqref{eq:zero-risk-variation},
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:aj-zero-risk-remainder}
|R_{X,n}|
\le \sum_{\ell}\sup_u|\Delta L_{n\ell}(u)|\,|Z_{n\ell}|(\tau)
=O_p(n^{-1/2})O_p(n^{-1})=O_p(n^{-3/2}).
\end{equation}

For each $\ell$, the process
$M_{n\ell}^{\nabla}(t)=\int_{(0,t]}\Delta L_{n\ell}(u)\,dU_{n\ell}(u)$
has a predictable integrand because $\Delta L_{n\ell}(u)$ uses only
$P_{\widehat A^{\textsf{AJ}}}(0,u-)$ and deterministic product integrals under $A_0$.
It is therefore a square-integrable martingale with predictable quadratic variation
bounded by

\[
\langle M_{n\ell}^{\nabla}\rangle(\tau) \le \frac1n\int_{(0,\tau]} \Delta L_{n\ell}(u)^2\frac{J_j(u)}{\bar Y_j(u)}\,dA_{\ell,0}(u).
\]

Set
$I_{n\ell}=\int_{(0,\tau]} \frac{J_j(u)}{\bar Y_j(u)}\,dA_{\ell,0}(u).$
The binomial bound \eqref{eq:binomial-inverse-bound} gives
$E I_{n\ell}\le C\int_{(0,\tau]} \frac{\1\{q_j(u)>0\}}{q_j(u)}\,dA_{\ell,0}(u)<\infty,$
and hence $I_{n\ell}=O_p(1)$. Therefore \eqref{eq:aj-coefficient-error-bound} and
\eqref{eq:aj-product-integral-rate} imply
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:aj-remainder-bracket}
\langle M_{n\ell}^{\nabla}\rangle(\tau)
\le \frac{C}{n}
\left(\sup_u|\Delta L_{n\ell}(u)|^2\right) I_{n\ell}
=O_p(n^{-2}).
\end{equation}
Lenglart's inequality and \eqref{eq:aj-remainder-bracket} give
$M_{n\ell}^{\nabla}(\tau)=O_p(n^{-1})$.
There are only three transitions, so $R_{U,n}=O_p(n^{-1})$. Together with
\eqref{eq:aj-zero-risk-remainder}, this gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:aj-rmst-remainder}
\widehat\mu^{\textsf{AJ}}-\mu_0-\dot\mu_{\tau,A_0}[\widehat A^{\textsf{AJ}}-A_0]
=O_p(n^{-1})=o_p(n^{-1/2}).
\end{equation}
The expansion \eqref{eq:aj-rmst-linearization} follows. Comparing
\eqref{eq:aj-rmst-remainder} with the exact expansion in
Lemma~\ref{lem:rmst-hazard-derivative} gives the equivalent assertion about the
product-integral remainder.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:weighted-na-linearization}
Fix a transition $\ell=(j,k)$.  Let $h_\ell$ be a bounded deterministic function
on $[0,\tau]$, and define
$L_\ell(u)=q_j(u)h_\ell(u).$
Under Assumption~\ref{ass:aj-main-integrated},
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:weighted-na-linearization}
\int_0^{\tau}
L_\ell(u)\,d\{\widehat A_\ell^{\textsf{AJ}}-A_{\ell,0}\}(u)
=
\int_0^{\tau}h_\ell(u)\,d\bar M_{\ell,0}(u)
+
O_p(n^{-1}).
\end{equation}
No lower bound on $q_j$ is required.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The Doob--Meyer decomposition
$d\bar N_\ell(u)=d\bar M_{\ell,0}(u)+\bar Y_j(u)dA_{\ell,0}(u),$
and the convention $J_j/\bar Y_j=0$ on $\bar Y_j=0$ give
$d\{\widehat A_\ell^{\textsf{AJ}}-A_{\ell,0}\}(u) = \frac{J_j(u)}{\bar Y_j(u)}d\bar M_{\ell,0}(u) +\{J_j(u)-1\}dA_{\ell,0}(u).$
Multiplication by $L_\ell=q_jh_\ell$ and addition and subtraction of $\int h_\ell d\bar M_{\ell,0}$ yield
\begin{align*}
\int L_\ell d(\widehat A_\ell^{\textsf{AJ}}-A_{\ell,0})
&=
\int h_\ell d\bar M_{\ell,0}+R_{1,n}+R_{2,n}, \\
R_{1,n}
&=
\int h_\ell(u)
\left\{\frac{q_j(u)J_j(u)}{\bar Y_j(u)}-1\right\}d\bar M_{\ell,0}(u), \\
R_{2,n}
&=
-\int q_j(u)h_\ell(u)\1\{\bar Y_j(u)=0\}dA_{\ell,0}(u).
\end{align*}
For $R_{2,n}$, boundedness $\|h_\ell\|_\infty<\infty$ implies
$E|R_{2,n}| \le \|h_\ell\|_\infty \int_0^{\tau}q_j(u)\Pr\{\bar Y_j(u)=0\}dA_{\ell,0}(u).$
At each fixed $u$, $K_u=n\bar Y_j(u)\sim \mathrm{Binomial}(n,q_j(u))$, and therefore $\Pr\{\bar Y_j(u)=0\}=\{1-q_j(u)\}^n\le e^{-nq_j(u)}$. Since $x e^{-nx}\le(en)^{-1}$,
$E|R_{2,n}| \le \frac{\|h_\ell\|_\infty}{en}A_{\ell,0}(\tau)=O(n^{-1}),$
so $R_{2,n}=O_p(n^{-1})$.

For $R_{1,n}$, the predictable quadratic variation satisfies
\begin{align*}
\langle R_{1,n}\rangle(\tau)
&\le
\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\int_0^{\tau}
 h_\ell(u)^2
\left\{\frac{q_j(u)J_j(u)}{\bar Y_j(u)}-1\right\}^2
Y_{j,i}(u)dA_{\ell,0}(u) \\
&=
\frac1n\int_0^{\tau}
 h_\ell(u)^2
\left\{\frac{q_j(u)J_j(u)}{\bar Y_j(u)}-1\right\}^2
\bar Y_j(u)dA_{\ell,0}(u).
\end{align*}
The integrand vanishes on $\{\bar Y_j(u)=0\}$, whereas on $\{\bar Y_j(u)>0\}$,
$\left\{\frac{q_jJ_j}{\bar Y_j}-1\right\}^2\bar Y_j = \frac{\{q_j-\bar Y_j\}^2}{\bar Y_j}.$
Thus
\begin{equation}
E\langle R_{1,n}\rangle(\tau)
 \le
\frac{\|h_\ell\|_\infty^2}{n}
\int_0^{\tau}
E\left[
\frac{\{q_j(u)-\bar Y_j(u)\}^2}{\bar Y_j(u)}\1\{\bar Y_j(u)>0\}
\right]
dA_{\ell,0}(u).\label{eq:weighted-na-bracket-bound}
\end{equation}
Let $K\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(n,q)$ and $\mu=nq$. Then
$E\left[ \frac{\{q-K/n\}^2}{K/n}\1\{K>0\} \right] = \frac1nE\left[\frac{(K-\mu)^2}{K}\1\{K>0\}\right] \le \frac{C}{n},$
where the last inequality follows by splitting on $\{K\ge \mu/2\}$, applying
Chernoff's bound on $\{K<\mu/2\}$, and handling $\mu<2$ using $(K-\mu)^2K^{-1}\1(K>0)\le2K+2\mu^2\1(K>0)$. Substitution in
\eqref{eq:weighted-na-bracket-bound} gives
$E\langle R_{1,n}\rangle(\tau) \le \frac{C\|h_\ell\|_\infty^2}{n^2}A_{\ell,0}(\tau)=O(n^{-2}).$
Doob's $L_2$ inequality implies $R_{1,n}=O_p(n^{-1})$. Combining this with $R_{2,n}=O_p(n^{-1})$
proves \eqref{eq:weighted-na-linearization}.

By Theorem~\ref{thm:aj-rmst-linearization},
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:aj-linearization-step}
\widehat\mu^{\textsf{AJ}}-\mu_0
=\dot\mu_{\tau,A_0}[\widehat A^{\textsf{AJ}}-A_0]+o_p(n^{-1/2}).
\end{equation}
The derivative coefficients in \eqref{eq:rmst-pathwise-derivative}
satisfy $L_\ell(u)=q_{j(\ell)}(u)H_{\ell,0}(u)$, because
$q_j(u)=P_j(u-)G(u-)$.
The functions $H_{\ell,0}$ in
\eqref{eq:main-nocov-rmst-H}
are bounded by \eqref{eq:rmst-weight-bound}. Thus
Lemma~\ref{lem:weighted-na-linearization}, applied to each transition, gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:aj-weighted-na-step}
\int_0^\tau L_\ell(u)\,d\{\widehat A_\ell^{\textsf{AJ}}-A_{\ell,0}\}(u)
=\int_0^\tau H_{\ell,0}(u)\,d\bar M_{\ell,0}(u)+O_p(n^{-1}).
\end{equation}
Summing over the three transitions in \eqref{eq:aj-linearization-step}
therefore yields
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:aj-influence-expansion}
\widehat\mu^{\textsf{AJ}}-\mu_0
=\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal J}\int_0^\tau H_{\ell,0}(u)\,d\bar M_{\ell,0}(u)
 +o_p(n^{-1/2}).
\end{equation}

Lemma~\ref{lem:aj-jump-regularity} gives continuous
compensators and excludes simultaneous transition jumps. Independence
across subjects and the resulting zero cross-variations imply
$\langle Z_n\rangle(t)=n^{-1}\sum_iR_i(t)$, where
$R_i(t)=\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal J}\int_0^tH_{\ell,0}(u)^2Y_{j(\ell),i}(u)\,dA_{\ell,0}(u)$.
The variables $R_i(\tau)$ are i.i.d. and integrable because the coefficients
are bounded and the hazard masses are finite. The law of large numbers and
the single-subject martingale isometry give
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:aj-bracket-limit}
\langle Z_n\rangle(\tau)\longrightarrow_p ER_1(\tau)
=\mathrm{Var}\{\phi^{

Moreover, the same lemma gives
$J_n^{\max}:=\max_{0<u\le\tau}\sum_{i,\ell}\Delta N_{\ell,i}(u)\le1$
almost surely. Continuity of the compensators therefore yields
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:aj-jump-bound}
\sup_{0<u\le\tau}|\Delta Z_n(u)|
\le H_{\max}J_n^{\max}/\sqrt n
\le H_{\max}/\sqrt n\longrightarrow0
\qquad\text{almost surely}.
\end{equation}
Rebolledo's martingale central limit theorem now gives
$Z_n(\tau)\rightsquigarrow N(0,\sigma_0^2)$.
Together with \eqref{eq:aj-martingale-terminal}, the asymptotic linear representation
just established, and Slutsky's theorem, this proves the normal limit in
Theorem~\ref{thm:aj-integrated-main}.
